why.correct: Lowering the administered rate lowers the flat part of reserve demand, so the federal funds rate falls; reserve supply, and so the quantity, stay put.
options: Reserve supply did not move, so the quantity of reserves is unchanged.
The flat part of demand moved down, so the rate where supply crosses it fell.
Right: the vertical supply now crosses demand at a lower flat part.
The flat part moved down, so the rate fell.

why.correct: A lower policy rate lowers other interest rates, which raises interest-sensitive spending such as business investment.
options: The quantity of reserves did not change; interest rates fell.
Right: a lower policy rate pulls other interest rates down, so more investment projects pay off.
Investment is interest sensitive: lower rates make borrowing cheaper.
Lower rates encourage borrowing and spending; investment rises.

why.correct: Lowering the policy rate is expansionary monetary policy, used to close a recessionary gap by raising aggregate demand.
options: A lower policy rate is expansionary: it raises aggregate demand, which would widen an inflationary gap.
Lower interest rates raise spending, so aggregate demand rises, not falls.
Raising AD in an inflationary gap would push prices higher; this policy fits a recession.
Right: lower rates raise investment and consumption, so AD shifts right and output rises.

why.correct: With limited reserves, selling bonds is contractionary: it lowers reserves and the money supply, raising interest rates.
options: Buying bonds does add reserves, but more reserves raise the money supply and push AD and prices higher: expansionary.
Selling is the right operation, but banks pay for the bonds with reserves, so reserves fall, not rise.
Right: banks pay for the bonds with reserves, so reserves and the money supply fall and interest rates rise.
The central bank pays for bonds it buys with new reserves, so buying adds reserves, and it is expansionary.

why.correct: Selling bonds takes reserves out of banks, so the money supply shifts left and the nominal interest rate rises.
Contractionary monetary policy raises interest rates, lowers interest-sensitive spending and shifts AD left, lowering the price level and real output.
options: Right: higher interest rates cut investment and consumption, so AD shifts left; the price level and real output fall.
Higher interest rates reduce spending, so AD falls, not rises.
A leftward shift of AD lowers both, not just the price level.
The money supply works through interest rates, which change investment and consumption, parts of AD.

why.correct: A central bank sale of bonds lowers bond prices and raises interest rates.
options: The central bank is adding bonds to the market, which pushes prices down.
Right: selling bonds pushes bond prices down, which is the same as interest rates rising.
The money supply falls through the bond sale itself, which lowers bond prices.
Bond prices move opposite to interest rates.

why.correct: With ample reserves, the central bank raises its policy rate by raising its administered rates.
options: In Year 2 reserves rose but the administered rates and the federal funds rate did not change.
Right: it raised both administered rates by half a point, and the federal funds rate rose with them.
In Year 4 reserves fell, but the administered rates and the policy rate stayed where Year 3 put them.
Year 1 is the starting point; there is no change to read.

why.correct: In the ample range, reserve demand is flat at the administered rate, so shifting reserve supply leaves the policy rate unchanged.
options: The issue is the shape of reserve demand, not a requirement.
$300 billion is large; the rate did not move because supply was already in the flat part of demand.
Right: with ample reserves, more reserves slide supply along the flat part, so the rate stays at the administered level.
Reserves did rise in the table, so nothing was canceled.

why.correct: Changes in the policy rate pass through to other interest rates, such as loan and mortgage rates.
options: Right: a higher policy rate raises banks' cost of funds and pulls other interest rates up.
The policy rate rose, so other rates tend to rise with it.
Reserves were the same, but the policy rate rose, and other rates follow it.
There is no reason for an early fall; rates move up with the policy rate.

why.correct: With ample reserves, the policy rate settles near the administered rates (between the overnight reverse repurchase rate and interest on reserve balances).
options: Big changes in reserves left the rate unchanged, which is the sign of ample reserves.
The table shows no reserve requirement; the rate follows the administered rates.
Banks short of reserves would bid the rate up, not hold it just below interest on reserves.
Right: the rate sits at the level the administered rates set and moves only when they move.

why.correct: The reserve market has the policy rate (the federal funds rate) on the vertical axis and the quantity of reserves on the horizontal axis, with reserve demand (DR) and a vertical reserve supply (SR). It is not the money market.
Raising the administered rate raises the flat part of reserve demand, so the federal funds rate rises; reserve supply, and the quantity of reserves, stay the same.
Adding reserves shifts reserve supply right, but in the flat part of reserve demand the policy rate stays at the administered rate; only the quantity of reserves rises.
Buying bonds adds reserves; banks lend the excess, so the money supply shifts right and the nominal interest rate falls.
Banks receive $20 million of new reserves with no new deposits, so all of it is excess. Money multiplier = 1 / 0.2 = 5, so the most the money supply can grow is $20 million x 5 = $100 million.
The discount rate is what the central bank charges banks for loans of reserves; lowering it is expansionary.
options: Cheaper borrowing from the central bank adds reserves, which raises the money supply.
The discount rate is the cost of borrowing reserves, so it changes bank lending.
More money lowers the nominal interest rate on the money market.
Right: banks borrow more reserves, lend more, and the money supply rises.

why.correct: Expansionary policy lowers interest rates: buying bonds, lowering the discount rate or the reserve ratio (limited reserves), or lowering administered rates (ample reserves).
options: Right: it adds reserves and raises the money supply.
Right: it lowers the flat part of reserve demand and the policy rate.
A higher ratio shrinks the money multiplier: contractionary.
Raising an administered rate raises the policy rate: contractionary.

why.correct: The federal funds rate, the rate on overnight loans of reserves between banks, is the Federal Reserve's policy rate.
options: Right: it is the Federal Reserve's policy rate.
That is a Treasury bond rate, which the policy rate influences but is not.
That is a bank lending rate, which moves with the policy rate.
That is an inflation target, not an interest rate.

why.correct: With ample reserves, administered rates (interest on reserve balances and the overnight reverse repurchase rate) set the policy rate.
options: With ample reserves, banks hold far more than required, so the ratio does not bind.
In the ample range, shifting reserve supply does not move the rate.
Right: the policy rate follows the rates the central bank pays.
That is fiscal policy, set by the government, not the central bank.

why.correct: Every link matters on the exam: the tool, the policy rate, other rates, interest-sensitive spending, AD, then output and unemployment.
Raising the administered rates raises the policy rate and other interest rates, which lowers investment and AD, so the price level falls (or rises more slowly).
The demand for loanable funds comes from borrowers: firms that invest, households and the government.
options: More saving shifts the supply of loanable funds right, not demand.
A change in the real interest rate moves along the curves; it does not shift them.
Right: government borrowing adds to the demand for loanable funds.
Gloomier firms borrow less, which shifts demand left.

why.correct: A rise in the demand for loanable funds raises the real interest rate and the quantity of loanable funds.
options: Right: more demand for a given supply of loanable funds raises their price, the real interest rate.
A rightward shift of demand along upward-sloping supply raises the rate.
The demand shift moves the equilibrium up along the supply curve.
The new equilibrium stays at the higher rate while the shift lasts.

why.correct: Government borrowing raises the real interest rate, and the higher rate lowers the quantity of private investment.
options: More is lent in total, but the government takes a bigger share at a higher real rate.
Firms' demand did not shift, but the higher real rate moves them along it to less borrowing.
Right: at the higher real rate, some private investment projects no longer pay off.
Government spending does not lower firms' borrowing costs; the higher real rate raises them.

why.correct: When demand shifts right along an upward-sloping supply curve, both the real interest rate and the quantity rise.
options: A higher rate cuts borrowing along the old demand, but here demand shifted right.
Saving rises along the supply curve as the real rate rises.
One curve shifted, so both changes are clear: the rate and the quantity rise.
Right: the higher real rate draws out more saving, a movement along supply.

why.correct: Public saving = tax revenue - government spending = 900 - 1,000 = -100 billion. The government spends more than it collects.
National saving = private saving + public saving = 400 + (-100) = 300 billion.
When public saving is negative, the government borrows, which adds to the demand for loanable funds (or, put the other way, lowers national saving).
options: Public saving is negative, so the government takes funds out rather than adding them.
Right: it spends $100 billion more than it collects and borrows the difference.
Government borrowing and saving are part of the market.
Private saving is given as 400; it is the government that borrows.

why.correct: Less government borrowing means more national saving and a lower real interest rate.
options: Public saving rises from -100 to 0, so national saving rises, not falls.
Right: with no government borrowing, there is less demand for loanable funds, so the real rate falls.
Public saving changed from -100 to 0, so national saving changes.
Less government borrowing lowers the real interest rate.

why.correct: More household saving shifts the supply of loanable funds right, so the real interest rate falls and the quantity of loanable funds rises.
More saving lowers the real interest rate, so the quantity of loanable funds borrowed for investment rises.
options: Right: cheaper borrowing makes more investment projects worth doing.
The loanable funds market shows the lower real rate raising investment.
Demand did not shift, but the lower real rate moves firms along it to more borrowing.
More saving lowers the real interest rate.

why.correct: Savers supply loanable funds; borrowers, such as investing firms and a government that spends more than it collects, demand them.
options: Firms that invest are borrowers: the demand side.
Right: saving is the supply of loanable funds.
The loanable funds market is about saving and borrowing; the policy rate is another graph.
Selling goods is not lending; savers supply loanable funds.

why.correct: Loanable funds: the real interest rate (vertical) and the quantity of loanable funds (horizontal), DLF sloping down and SLF up. Along DLF a lower real rate means more borrowing, so C sits down and to the right of the equilibrium.
More planned investment means more borrowing at each real rate: the demand for loanable funds shifts right, raising the real interest rate and the quantity of loanable funds.
Along SLF, a higher real interest rate draws out more saving, so B sits up and to the right of the equilibrium.
Loanable funds: real interest rate (r) on the vertical axis. Writing "nominal" loses the graph point.
options: The nominal rate goes on the money market graph. Saving and borrowing decisions depend on the real rate.
That goes on the horizontal axis.
The price level goes on the AD-AS graph.
Right: savers and borrowers care about the return and cost after inflation.

why.correct: Demand for loanable funds shifts with borrowing plans: government borrowing and firms' expected returns on investment.
options: Right: the government becomes a bigger borrower.
Gloomier firms borrow less at each real rate, a shift to the left.
More saving shifts supply right, not demand.
That is a movement along demand, not a shift.

why.correct: Saving responds to the reward for saving, the real interest rate: a higher rate brings out more loanable funds.
options: Right: the real rate is the reward for saving.
No rule makes banks lend more; savers choose to supply more at higher rates.
The real rate already removes inflation; the slope comes from savers' choices.
Public saving depends on taxes and spending, not on the slope of supply.

why.correct: Government borrowing raises the real interest rate, and the higher rate lowers private investment.
Government borrowing raises the demand for loanable funds, the real interest rate rises, and private investment falls because borrowing costs more.
